correctness.rationale: For \(n\ge3\) each side of a feasible function has at least two positive vertices. One-side assignments are partitioned exhaustively into robust weight at least four (or three ones), weak weight two (two ones), and weak weight three (one two and one one). Missing matched neighbors turn the two weak cases into forced-positive conditions. \(F_{1,n}\) and \(F_{2,n}\) remove all nonrobust states with specified positive indices. Counting the six exhaustive pairings gives exactly the stated polynomial and has no double counting. Coefficient and evaluation identities follow. An independent adjacency-based exhaustive verifier checked all 597780 ternary assignments across \(n=3,4,5,6\), and polynomial identities through \(n=60\); finite checks are not used as the infinite proof.

broader_coverage.reasoning: For \(n\ge3\) the crown graph is not complete multipartite: same-side vertices are nonadjacent, but each opposite-side vertex is adjacent to all except its matched counterpart. Removing an entire perfect matching destroys the homogeneous cross-part condition and changes zero feasibility. An inequality for minimum weight or a closed polynomial on \(K_{n,n}\) cannot imply the requested enumerator on \(\(K_{n,n}\)-M\). No broad theorem in inspected primary material supplies such a coefficient-preserving reduction.

value.rationale: The complete weight profile on a natural infinite vertex-transitive bipartite family is an enumerative invariant not determined by general numerical domination bounds. A compact finite expression counts all feasible assignments at any budget, with a nontrivial six-regime interplay between low-support sides and precise corrections for the deleted matching. It yields exact minimum/next-minimum multiplicities, a closed total count and exponential rejection asymptotics, rather than a routine scalar minimum alone.
